# Tuples

Tuples are lightweight anonymous product types.

> **Gap** GAP-TYPES-009

```metel
fun main() -> i64 {
    let coord: (i64, i64) := (10, 20);
    let triple: (String, i64, boolean) := ("yes", 42, true);
    return coord.0 + triple.1;
}
```

Positional field access [uses zero-based selectors `.0`, `.1`, etc.](#spec.types.tuples.legality-1):

```metel
fun main() -> i64 {
    let coord: (i64, i64) := (10, 20);
    let x := coord.0;
    let y := coord.1;
    return x + y;
}
```

`()` is the zero-element tuple (unit type), the empty closed row `.{}`, so `()` and `.{}` are one type ([the empty tuple](#spec.types.tuples.legality-2)).

Tuples can be destructured in `match`:

```metel
fun main() -> i64 {
    let coord: (i64, i64) := (10, 0);
    match (coord) {
        (0, y) => y,
        (x, 0) => x,
        (x, y) => x + y,
    }
}
```

<details>
<summary>Formal rules</summary>

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.tuples.legality-1}

A tuple's elements are addressed by zero-based positional selectors. A selector is valid
only for an element in the tuple's declared arity.

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 7aae970193f94e38bc185aef533ec5db127b3c47 -->

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.tuples.legality-2}

`()` is the empty closed row `.{}`: one type and one value, not a separate primitive. A function with no return
annotation, an empty block, a block with no tail, a braceless `if` without `else`, and a `break` with no value have this type.
`()` and `.{}` are interchangeable in type position and in pattern position, `Result<(), E>` and `Result<.{}, E>` are one type,
and both literals denote the one value. A branded empty residual `Name.{}` is not `()`: its brand is part of its type.

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 6fecc8dcbfdd36500a77b2f6139e5f5ef970ce10 -->

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.tuples.legality-3}

`extend (): A` is accepted as a spelling of `extend .{}: A`. Writing both is a `T0015` conflicting implementation.
`Copy` and `Clone` of `()` come from the row impls that hold vacuously for the empty row.

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 5cf937885aa1d7b45b93bb5477397ab486fe161c -->


##### Dynamic Semantics Rule {#spec.types.tuples.dynamics-1}

The empty row prints as `()`, as a type and as a value, so `println(.{})`, `println(())` and `"${.{}}"` all produce `()`.

`()` and `.{}` are one type with one value ([the empty tuple](#spec.types.tuples.legality-2)), so the language has exactly one
rendering for it, and the rendering is the unit's: the record `Display` has a single case for the empty row, where it would
otherwise print the record form `.{}`. Every non-empty anonymous record prints as its source form
([Display of an anonymous record](records/projection.md#spec.types.anonymous-records.dynamics-3)); the empty one is the only exception. A diagnostic
that names the type writes `()` for the same reason.

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 5cf937885aa1d7b45b93bb5477397ab486fe161c -->

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.tuples.legality-4}

A tuple type `(A₀, …, Aₙ)` is the closed anonymous record type `.{ .0: A₀, …, .n: Aₙ }`, and a tuple value `(a₀, …, aₙ)` is the record `.{ .0 = a₀, … }`: they are one type and one value, not a distinct form. `t.i` is field access on the label `.i`, and a tuple pattern is a pattern over the same labels. A tuple is therefore subject to every rule of a record: narrowing, row bounds, and the row impls of `Copy`, `Clone` and `Display`. A tuple carries no brand.

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 6fecc8dcbfdd36500a77b2f6139e5f5ef970ce10 -->

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.tuples.legality-5}

`(x,)` is the one-element tuple `.{ .0 = x }`, its type is written `(T,)`, and a pattern `(p,)` matches it. `(e)` and `(T)` without the trailing comma are parenthesised groupings and are not tuples. `()` is the empty tuple ([the empty tuple](#spec.types.tuples.legality-2)).

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 8156f9b70d40f62450255e0a8c9ce9c1af2d21b4 -->

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.tuples.legality-6}

A row's labels are integers or identifiers, written `.0`, `.name`. The canonical order of a row's labels, for iteration, display and derived comparison, is its integer labels first in numeric order (`.2` before `.10`), then its identifier labels in lexicographic order. A row may mix the two kinds (`.{ .0: A, .name: B }`): a call's argument list is such a row, with positional arguments as integer labels and keyword arguments as identifier labels. The `(…)` sugar produces only the dense integer labels `.0 .. .N-1`; a mixed row is written with `.{ … }`.

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 8156f9b70d40f62450255e0a8c9ce9c1af2d21b4 -->

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.tuples.legality-7}

A closed row is a **`Tuple`** when its labels are exactly the integers `.0 .. .N-1`. The property is decided by inspecting the row, with no annotation or proof, and it adds no rule for ownership, narrowing or aspects. A `Tuple` row prints as `(T₀, …, Tₙ)`, a one-element one as `(T,)` and the empty one as `()`; any other row, including one with a gap in its integer labels or an identifier label, prints in brace form `.{ … }`. A row that stops being a `Tuple`, as a partial move that leaves a gap does, loses that rendering and nothing else.

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 8156f9b70d40f62450255e0a8c9ce9c1af2d21b4 -->

Equality, ordering and hashing of a tuple are those of every row: the fields compared in canonical label order, positional for integer labels. They arrive with operator dispatch through aspects; until then `==` and `<` apply only to primitive operands, which excludes a tuple as it does any other non-primitive type.

<!-- rfc.py:origins:start -->

##### Legality Rule {#spec.types.tuples.legality-8}

A tuple element access `t.n` names the integer label `n` of the tuple's row. An index that is not a
label of that row is a type error (`T0003`, out of bounds).

<!-- rfc.py:last_reviewed 7aae970193f94e38bc185aef533ec5db127b3c47 -->
